items.title: mini-psych-agent: Evaluating Human-Like Behavior in LLM Agents through Interactive Psychological Environments
items.abstract: A Large Language Model (LLM), its harness, and the test-time compute budget jointly determine its behavior. Consequently, the same underlying model, embedded in different agentic workflows or allocated different amounts of test-time compute, can exhibit markedly different performance. Psychologists face an analogous challenge when evaluating human performance: the same person may behave differently under different incentives and levels of deliberation. Psychological tasks therefore provide an ideal testbed for studying such behavioral variation. However, when adapted to LLMs, these tasks are typically text-transcribed, replaying fixed, language-rendered experiments as static prompts. This format is ill-suited to agent evaluation, where actions can alter future observations and task states. Conversely, although dynamic environments are prevalent in the evaluation of LLM agents, they rarely ask whether the resulting behavior is human-like. Here, we bridge this gap by transforming psychological tasks into dynamic environments in which agents can interact and by using a learned human-policy model to evaluate how compatible the resulting behavioral trajectories are with human behavior. Across these environments, we find that this compatibility varies with an LLM's agentic configuration and the psychological task, and that memory raises it mainly by making choices more predictable rather than more human-like. These findings motivate a more holistic evaluation of LLM agents in psychology-inspired environments, accounting for both the backbone model and its agentic scaffold.

items.title: Tacinf: A Unified Tactile Infrastructure for Robot Manipulation
items.abstract: Force-aware manipulation requires robots to infer appropriate interaction forces from task context and tactile feedback. We present Tacinf, a low-cost, modular infrastructure that enables policies to predict robot actions and fingertip forces from task language, vision, and touch. Task instructions can optionally specify the desired force level. Tacinf integrates simulation data synthesis and tactile benchmarking (Tabero), vision-tactile-language-action (VTLA) policy learning, handheld data collection using the same gripper as robot deployment (Tacumi), and task-aligned sim-to-real evaluation (Taco). Together, these components form an integrated workflow connecting data collection from multiple sources, foundation-model training, and hardware deployment. We validate each component, including the simulation data, benchmark, controller, and Tacumi, and are releasing the full stack as open source. A foundation model fine-tuned solely on tactile simulation data transfers zero-shot to different real-robot tasks. Across eight policy variants, mean task success rates are strongly correlated between simulation and the real robot (Pearson r=0.998, mean maximum rank violation MMRV=0.010). For the four policies with reported force measurements, mean grip force is higher under firm instructions than under gentle instructions on all three tasks in both domains. When both object positions and instances are randomized, a mixture of teleoperation, simulation, and Tacumi data raises mean real-robot task success from 20% with teleoperation alone to 60%.

items.title: Do You Even Know What I Want? Improving LLMs Ability to Detect Hidden User Intent
items.abstract: As with conventional AI agents, a common source of misalignment between Large Language Models (LLMs) and their human users is misspecified goals. Often, this happens when the human has skewed beliefs about the system's model and provides it with information that causes behavior different from what they expected, with potentially unwanted side effects. To ensure goal alignment, one solution would be for the LLM to ask the human questions about their objectives. However, it has been well-documented that LLMs most often provide default responses to user requests rather than try and ask questions to clarify their true intent. In this paper, we address these challenges by adapting a novel formulation for the objective misspecification problem to work with LLMs. We then test if LLMs that are prompted to ask questions about a user's true underlying objectives are better at identifying them compared to those that do not. We evaluate our method using four state-of-the-art LLMs tested on five standard IPC domains, showing that for some domains, asking questions greatly improved model performance.

items.title: Interrogation Protocols for AI Control
items.abstract: As the intelligence of an AI agent increases relative to a trusted monitor, so does the risk that the monitor will fail to understand the agent's actions or to evaluate them confidently. We introduce interrogation protocols to a high-stakes AI control setting, and allow the monitor to ask the untrusted agent questions about confusing actions. For interrogation to improve safety, a weaker model must be able to distinguish misleading explanations produced by an attack policy from genuine ones produced by an honest policy. We find that on a held-out subset of BashArena, an interrogation protocol improves safety at a 1% audit budget from 72.6% for an actions-only baseline, which does not use interrogations, to 79.5% (+7.0 pp [+0.9, +20.1], 95% paired bootstrap interval), but most of this uplift can be captured by having a trusted model state a specific concern. More broadly, our work suggests that interrogating agents can improve safety, allowing monitors to catch more attacks at a larger capability gap.

items.title: Tether: Verified Stateful Policy Engine for System-Level Monitoring of Agents
items.abstract: Autonomous AI agents are increasingly deployed for long-running tasks that execute arbitrary shell commands or programs. However, these actions can result in unauthorized network requests or persistent, malicious changes to the user's file system, processes, or privileges. Existing defense mechanisms rely on either LLM-based monitors, which lack provable safety guarantees, or stateless policy enforcement layers, which miss multi-step data flows and execution side-effects unmodeled by the policy language (e.g., network calls initiated inside a Python script). We introduce Tether, a framework for runtime enforcement of stateful security policies over the observed side-effects of an agent's actions. Tether executes each proposed action in an ephemeral, isolated sandbox, inferring abstract action semantics from observed system calls. Tether then enforces stateful policies over these inferred semantics, permitting actions to proceed only if they comply with the policy. Policies and action semantics are defined in an embedded DSL in Lean 4 capable of expressing diverse constraints, including information flow control (IFC), access control, and network security policies. Because actions can propagate labels from sources to destinations, a single rule can enforce fine-grained IFC policies across multi-step execution flows of arbitrary length. Expressing policies in Lean enables formal verification that they satisfy global security invariants (e.g., preventing network access after reading a sensitive file). We evaluate Tether on realistic coding-agent benchmarks across both benign and adversarial trajectories. With a single policy shared across all tasks, Tether blocks 100% of in-scope attacks while maintaining a benign false-positive rate under 5%.

items.title: When Agents Play Differently: Localizing Human--Agent Behavioral Divergence with Conditional Distributional Testing
items.abstract: Evaluating whether artificial agents behave like humans requires comparing not just average outcomes but entire behavioral distributions across diverse contexts. We propose a stratified framework that computes nonparametric discrepancy statistics within contextual cells, and discovers subgroup rules identifying where agent behavior departs from human play. We show that session-level metrics dominated by win/loss outcomes offer little signal beyond mean comparisons, whereas process-level metrics such as move efficiency reveal genuine behavioral differences. Applied to a commercial match-3 game, it uncovers patterns invisible to aggregate metrics: a playtesting bot is diverging substantially from humans in certain game modes, while showing no detectable divergence in others. We release our implementation as open source to support reproducibility and adoption.

items.title: An Experimental Apparatus for Embodied Conversational AI: A Simple Implementation Coupling a Commercial Voice AI with an Avatar
items.abstract: As generative AI becomes integrated into everyday life, understanding how avatars shape human-AI interaction and the perception of AI as a social partner is becoming increasingly important. This paper builds a research instrument on audio-output coupling, which connects the audio output of a generative AI to an external avatar. There are two implementations: the browser implementation captures the audio of a tab selected through screen sharing without installing additional software, and the desktop implementation captures the audio of the service embedded in the application. Both work with the voice AI as people ordinarily use it, and as a method neither depends on a particular service. The implementation reported here, Deskmate, generates speech state, mouth shape, and expression from low-level features such as voice-band mean amplitude, RMS, peak, and transients. Because it uses no microphone, speech recognition, or transcription, Deskmate acquires neither the user's voice nor the content of the conversation. Records of the conversation remain with the voice AI provider, but none are kept automatically on the side of Deskmate. Three interchangeable backends are provided for rendering the avatar: 3D (VRM), 2D (Live2D), and CSS. Deskmate allows researchers to manipulate avatar presentation as an experimental condition, without changing the commercial service's interface, voice, or response generation. Because conversation content is not held fixed, the estimand is the total effect, including the changes in the participant's speech and the AI's responses that the presentation brings about. A server edition, served from the researcher's server for online experiments, is also provided. The effectiveness of avatar presentation has not yet been evaluated; this paper reports the design and implementation.

items.title: Co-Defining Transparency for Clinical AI: A Replicable Participatory Methodology
items.abstract: Transparency is the most invoked safeguard for clinical AI, yet frameworks (e.g. the EU AI Act, FUTURE-AI) are specified top-down by regulators and technical experts, not bottom-up by the frontline users whose trust and adoption they should calibrate. This disconnect exacerbates the central deployment failure of clinical AI, miscalibrated reliance and adoption (such as automation bias, deskilling, or disuse), which technical explanation alone does not resolve. We argue that "how much transparency, of what kind, and for whom" is an empirical, context-dependent question, and present a replicable participatory methodology to answer it, instantiated at a large European university hospital. A cumulative chain of six workshops engages an inter-professional panel (clinicians, patient and caregiver partners, students) in agnostic, open-ended elicitation: 274 stakeholder verbatims and external benchmarks (eCH-0272, EU AI Act, Stanford FMTI) yield 20 indicators (18 prioritised and 2 recovered at a later stage), rated across five clinical scenarios of graduated intervention before and after technical briefings, discussed with legal experts, and translated into concrete implementation features. As an existence proof, the use case yields decision-useful signals: human review of automated decisions is the single most critical transparency indicator (84% of participants), and required transparency for adoption rises monotonically with the perceived risk of intervention, corroborating WHO risk-proportionality. A short explainability briefing did not substantially shift participants' transparency requirements. Of 151 evaluated AI transparency solutions, 79 were accepted as-is, covering (at least partially) 17 out of the 20 selected indicators. We position the six-workshop protocol (not its single-site outcomes) as the transferable artefact and release all instruments to support replication.

items.title: EA-Bench: Measuring information and action efficiency under imperfect instructions
items.abstract: Personal agents help users complete everyday work across digital applications. Many standard benchmarks assume that users provide sufficient information to solve a task. However, agents often encounter incomplete, distracting, or inconsistent information in practice. To systematically study agent inefficiency under such imperfect information, we introduce Efficient Action (EA)-Bench, which evaluates both tool calls and user interactions in work-related tasks. To our knowledge, it is the first benchmark to jointly evaluate tool-call efficiency and user-interaction efficiency under controlled missing, redundant, and conflicting information. We construct 63 base-task instances adapted from existing work-related benchmarks. To guide perturbation design and quantify task requirements, we represent workflows as directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) and examine node-level dependencies to identify where information can be withheld, contradicted, or supplemented with distractors. We use a two-stage validation process combining AI-assisted checks with expert screening to select 232 conditions from 792 initial candidates. We organize these tasks into Easy and Hard tracks by task complexity. Experiments show that imperfect information can reduce accuracy and increase tool-use and user-interaction costs. More concerning, several models obtain apparently correct outcomes by guessing user-specific values without confirmation, revealing potential execution unreliability in current models under imperfect user information.

items.title: Grounding Collaborative Agents in Group Cognition
items.abstract: Collaborative agents joining an ongoing team rely on shared context to connect multi-party interaction histories with downstream coordination decisions. Existing work typically focuses either on retrieving historical facts from conversation logs, which surfaces isolated evidence without capturing who knows or owns what, or on evaluating end-to-end interactions, which conflates preparation with execution and lacks direct supervision because a team's history has no single ground-truth summary. To bridge this gap, we formulate group briefing, the task of reconstructing task-relevant group cognition across participants' expressed beliefs, group dynamics, and grounding gaps, and introduce a four-domain benchmark of 1,351 requests and 9,975 verified reference points paired with a two-stage evaluation pipeline combining reference-point coverage and downstream collaboration simulation. Using this pipeline, we show that GroupBrief, a simple task-guided approach that iteratively probes the message history and synthesizes a structured brief without offline memory indexing or graph construction, outperforms ten retrieval and agent-memory baselines in overall coverage with gpt-5.4-mini, while benchmarking nine language models reveals that prospective friction remains harder to recover than past state across model scales. We further use reference-point coverage as a feedback signal for harness optimization, refining GroupBrief's retrieval and synthesis instructions while keeping model weights frozen. On held-out Test projects, GroupBrief (optimized) improves coverage by 2.54 percentage points for gpt-5.4-mini and 12.88 for gpt-5.6-luna, achieving 64.46% and 68.42% preference over no brief in downstream simulations. These results establish our benchmark and evaluation pipeline as a foundation for measuring and optimizing how collaborative agents ground in group cognition.

items.title: RUIBench: What Makes a Good Robot-Use Interface?
items.abstract: Foundation models can reason about complex physical tasks, yet translating this intelligence into reliable robot execution remains challenging. We argue that a critical, often overlooked factor is the robot-use interface (RUI), which determines how agents express and execute physical actions. To systematically study its impact, we introduce RUIBench, comprising 30 manipulation tasks across five suites spanning world knowledge, in-context learning, discovery, dynamic interaction, and contact-rich manipulation. We further develop RUIKit, a unified framework that crosses six action abstractions with two interaction forms, yielding 13 interfaces under shared perception and control. In simulation, changing only the RUI shifts a frontier agent's success rate from 45% to 81%, and that of a fine-tuned 4B model from 13% to 47%. Our analysis reveals that effective interfaces reduce unnecessary decisions while preserving essential feedback, with their benefits shaped by agent behavior and physical uncertainty. We further uncover a verification gap, where agents frequently declare success despite observable failures, revealing the need for task-level verification beyond individual actions. Together, these findings establish RUI design as a critical factor in embodied agent reliability.

items.title: Don't Sleep, Keep Watch: Proactive Perception for Computer-Use Agents
items.abstract: Computer-use agents (CUAs) built on vision-language models are increasingly entrusted with long-horizon tasks in live desktop, web, and mobile environments, where the screen keeps changing on its own. However, current CUAs lack real-time situational awareness: they perceive the environment through discrete snapshots, and the substantial inference latency of VLMs, compounded by highly dynamic interfaces, opens a perception-action gap in which the observed state frequently becomes stale before the corresponding action is executed. To bridge this gap, we present NightWatch, a plug-and-play framework that endows any CUA with continuous, temporally grounded perception without changing the agent's model, prompt, or action space. NightWatch couples the VLM agent with NightWatch-0.8B, a lightweight System-1 model that performs streaming monitoring of the interface state and keeps the agent synchronized with the evolving environment at low computational cost and latency, thereby grounding each decision in the current state rather than an outdated snapshot and reducing both stale actions and idle waiting while preserving task success. Experiments on desktop and dynamic web environments (OSWorld-Verified and DynaCU-Bench) show that NightWatch, driven by a watcher of only 0.8B parameters, reduces non-reasoning wall-clock time by 33% and wasted time by 53% on OSWorld while keeping task success on par, raises success on DynaCU-Bench from 39.5% to 44.2% with the large VLM agent, and is more efficient than passive-watching baselines such as AOI and PUSV under the same screenshot-only input, as well as a System-1 decision model more than $30\times$ its size. Overall, NightWatch demonstrates that the timing of perception is as critical as its content, marking a step toward agents that maintain continuous awareness of their environment rather than perceiving it turn by turn.

items.title: Embodied Human-Data Interaction
items.abstract: We propose the concept of human-data interaction (HDI) as the human manipulation, analysis, and sensemaking of large, unstructured, and complex datasets. We illustrate our approach with two examples: tangible lenses for visual exploration, and an educational computer game with tangible bricks.

items.title: Emotion-Aware and Context-Grounded Dialogue Agents for Personalized Video Game Interactions
items.abstract: We present ChatNPC, a game companion that dynamically personalizes its responses in real time based on players' emotional shifts to enhance user immersion. The model integrates sequential data, leveraging the dynamic nature of streams to benefit from player information, spoken lines, and in-game context. We leverage recent progress in LLMs' tool-calling capabilities to extract vital information from memory and recognize potential constraints for accurate reasoning, thereby tackling the complexity of NPC conversation scenarios. The task is divided into a game sentinel-guided agent (SeGent), a memory capability, and a chat planning tool for reasoning instantiation. The approach uses a lightweight game template as an information framework, with relevant details and a thorough reasoning layout. We conduct extensive experiments on a newly developed game dataset for in-game context NPC dialogue and demonstrate that ChatNPC sequentially captures players' emotional shifts over time; responses are more naturalistic and human-like with appropriate conversational cues, pauses, and sighs; and utterances remain faithful to the dynamics of in-game context and player actions, supporting narrative continuity.

items.title: COGENT: A Modular Cognitive Architecture for Agentic User Simulation
items.abstract: LLM-based user simulation can support interface design, accessibility research, and interactive-agent evaluation, but standard computer-use agents are optimized for task completion rather than reproducing how people perceive, reason, and act. We introduce COGENT (COGnitive agENT), a modular cognitive architecture for simulating user interaction with desktop interfaces. COGENT draws on established cognitive theories, such as Norman's action cycle and ACT-R, to enable explainable, intervenable, and modular user simulation by decomposing the simulation process into cognitive modules with explicit representations of perception, memory, user state, intentions, and action selection. We begin by presenting six intervenability demonstrations, each tracing how a single edit to memory, a user attribute, or a processing module propagates through the cognitive pipeline to produce a behavioral change. We evaluate COGENT's behavioral and attributional fidelity across three benchmarks -- AgentNetBench, A11y-CUA, and SENSE-42 -- finding that it achieves statistically significant fidelity gains over computer-use baselines in reproducing recorded human behavior and recovers the relational structure among human self-reported psychological states. Together, these demos and evaluations demonstrate COGENT's utility toward more faithful, explainable, intervenable, and modular LLM-based cognitive simulations.

items.title: One Style Fits All? Cultural Values Embedded in Conversational AI via a People-Pleasing Lens
items.abstract: Conversational AI systems trained on large-scale web corpora inevitably encode the cultural values and interactional norms embedded in their training data, yet our understanding of how deployed LLMs reflect or reinforce culture-specific social expectations remains limited. This study examined how supportive versus challenging chatbot interaction styles shape user experience and continuance intention, and whether people-pleasing tendency (PPT) moderates these effects across cultures. Taiwanese (N = 49) and Korean (N = 52) participants completed a collaborative tourism-planning task. Results showed that: (1) supportive chatbots consistently led to higher continuance intention, satisfaction, and trust; (2) PPT did not moderate these effects; and (3) cultural variation emerged only in perceived threat, where higher PPT was associated with greater baseline threat in the Taiwanese but not the Korean sample. These findings reveal how a general-purpose LLM style may differentially activate culturally situated social scripts, raising implications for culturally inclusive conversational AI design.

items.title: Interactive Neural Computers
items.abstract: Computers and their interfaces are usually treated as fixed, so a person, or increasingly an AI agent, must adapt to whatever the operating system presents. This is limiting when someone needs a different workflow, or an interface suited to hands-free use or a disability. We explore an overlooked alternative. Rather than training an agent to operate an existing computer, we train a generative model to be the computer, predicting each next screen from past screens and the user's mouse and keyboard actions. Treating a desktop as an interactive world model raises problems that natural-video world models largely avoid. Without a camera pose to index memory, the model must remember content that has left the screen without any geometric cues. Arithmetic in a terminal has to be exactly right, not merely plausible. Small interface text must also stay legible at interactive frame rates. Our Interactive Neural Computer is structured like a Neural Turing Machine and starts to address these problems with three modules trained end to end from pixels and actions. A surprise-gated slot memory, supervised by latent next-frame prediction (MEMORY-JEPA), stores what is off screen. An exploratory query bridge brings in the reasoning of a pretrained VLM, and a residual renderer predicts only the latent changes between frames. In long closed-loop rollouts, our model recalls occluded files in 64.2% of trials (chance is 33.3%), compared with at most 56.0% for recurrent and sliding-window baselines. It also raises terminal-text OCR accuracy from 1.3% to 50.1%. Finally, because the memory is explicit, it can be transplanted at test time to causally change what the model renders.

items.title: SecondChance: Benchmarking Reliable Error Recovery in AI Agents
items.abstract: AI agents make errors while they act, and their reliability depends on what they do afterwards. Existing recovery benchmarks mostly inject faults, involve no user and score whether the task is eventually completed, so they cannot show whether an agent undid its own silent error, told the user, or faced an error that could not be fixed. We introduce SecondChance, an error checkpoint dataset and evaluation harness that profiles and measures error-recovery behaviour of AI agents. The errors are natural: they come from agents' own task attempts in $τ^2$-bench, BFCL and AppWorld. Different agents then resume from the same checkpoints under one of four conditions: no assistance, an error notice, the error location, or repair guidance. We measure error correction, task success, policy compliance, preservation of environment state, repair durability and cost. We evaluate 12 models under all four conditions in 5,760 continuations. Recovery is rare: across its environments, the best model completes only 16% of recoveries unaided and 27% with repair guidance. Correcting is not recovering: with repair guidance, Llama-3.3-70B corrects 26% of $τ^2$ errors but completes none, and 40 of 84 successful AppWorld continuations leave the error in place. SecondChance exposes these differences that task success alone cannot capture.

items.title: TACT-Bench: Testing Adaptive Conversational Threats against Tool-Use Agents
items.abstract: The growing autonomy of AI agents in using external tools and making decisions has created an urgent need for comprehensive safety benchmarks. Existing benchmarks test compromised tool channels or adaptive multi-turn attacks, though they may not capture the unique capabilities of policy-governed tool-use agents, which must resist unauthorized requests without abandoning the legitimate work embedded in the same interaction. To fill this gap, we introduce TACT-Bench, a stateful benchmark built around scenario-specific stories, personas, manipulation tactics, and response-adaptive escalation. Each adversarial task targets an action explicitly prohibited by the policy provided to the assistant, while the policy remains hidden from the attacking user. TACT pairs each adversarial task with at least one benign counterpart, and its adversarial tasks retain authorized ground-truth actions when a compliant resolution remains available. We define these base tasks as TACT-Base. We additionally introduce TACT-TrustPrime, which places an independent benign task before an unrelated attack in the same conversation. We also propose Paired Selective Trustworthiness (PST), which combines explicit safe refusal with demonstrated capability on matched benign tasks, to analyze an agent's overcautiousness and practicality. Averaged across 6 different models as assistants, TACT-Base raises Attack-Induced Failure Rate (AFR) by 17.53% over four compatible attack baselines, and TACT-TrustPrime raises it by a further 17.01%. The two evaluated defense methods reduce AFR by only 8.35%--9.41% on average and do not consistently improve PST, underscoring the need for stronger policy-enforcement methods.

items.title: E2SIM: Long-Horizon Simulation of Everyday Human Behavior with Evolving States
items.abstract: AI agents are increasingly expected to support users over long periods, across work, and daily life. This requires modeling not only who users are, but also how their goals, interests, activities, and interactions evolve over time. A challenge in longitudinal user simulation is maintaining consistency between these evolving states and the consequences of actions in a shared environment. We introduce E2SIM, a longitudinal user simulation framework that jointly models evolving actor states and a dynamic shared environment. E2SIM connects actor-state updates with shared-world changes through a feedback loop linking immediate actions, delayed outcomes, and actor-specific observations across work and life. This allows the consequences of earlier actions to shape later behavior, while preserving differences in what each actor knows. We further propose a suite of longitudinal trajectory diagnostics, measuring dynamic consistency, coherent event progression and collaboration, and non-degenerate trajectory development rather than static consistency alone. In one 60-day simulation, E2SIM produced more extracted event threads judged meaningful by our evaluator and fewer near-duplicate actions than four direct-generation baselines. The framework and evaluation methods provide a basis for studying longitudinal user simulation, with potential applications in training and evaluating AI agents that assist users over extended periods.

items.title: Tether: Verified Stateful Policy Engine for System-Level Monitoring of Agents
items.abstract: Autonomous AI agents are increasingly deployed for long-running tasks that execute arbitrary shell commands or programs. However, these actions can result in unauthorized network requests or persistent, malicious changes to the user's file system, processes, or privileges. Existing defense mechanisms rely on either LLM-based monitors, which lack provable safety guarantees, or stateless policy enforcement layers, which miss multi-step data flows and execution side-effects unmodeled by the policy language (e.g., network calls initiated inside a Python script). We introduce Tether, a framework for runtime enforcement of stateful security policies over the observed side-effects of an agent's actions. Tether executes each proposed action in an ephemeral, isolated sandbox, inferring abstract action semantics from observed system calls. Tether then enforces stateful policies over these inferred semantics, permitting actions to proceed only if they comply with the policy. Policies and action semantics are defined in an embedded DSL in Lean 4 capable of expressing diverse constraints, including information flow control (IFC), access control, and network security policies. Because actions can propagate labels from sources to destinations, a single rule can enforce fine-grained IFC policies across multi-step execution flows of arbitrary length. Expressing policies in Lean enables formal verification that they satisfy global security invariants (e.g., preventing network access after reading a sensitive file). We evaluate Tether on realistic coding-agent benchmarks across both benign and adversarial trajectories. With a single policy shared across all tasks, Tether blocks 100% of in-scope attacks while maintaining a benign false-positive rate under 5%.

items.title: When Agents Play Differently: Localizing Human--Agent Behavioral Divergence with Conditional Distributional Testing
items.abstract: Evaluating whether artificial agents behave like humans requires comparing not just average outcomes but entire behavioral distributions across diverse contexts. We propose a stratified framework that computes nonparametric discrepancy statistics within contextual cells, and discovers subgroup rules identifying where agent behavior departs from human play. We show that session-level metrics dominated by win/loss outcomes offer little signal beyond mean comparisons, whereas process-level metrics such as move efficiency reveal genuine behavioral differences. Applied to a commercial match-3 game, it uncovers patterns invisible to aggregate metrics: a playtesting bot is diverging substantially from humans in certain game modes, while showing no detectable divergence in others. We release our implementation as open source to support reproducibility and adoption.

items.title: MERIT: Experience-Guided Memory for Long-Horizon Persona-Specific Persuasive Dialogue
items.abstract: Effective long-horizon persuasion in recurring goal-oriented settings requires more than factual memory: it must track how a user's trust, negotiation behavior, and strategic receptiveness evolve across interactions. Existing persuasive dialogue systems are largely single-session, static, and unimodal, while cross-session memory systems, though temporally aware, retain only factual content and overlook persuasion-specific dynamics. We propose MERIT (Memory-augmented Experience-Rationale for Iterative Temporal persuasion), which pairs a graph-based memory of four persuasion-specific memory types with a per-persona experience rationale library that records which strategies succeed for each user and why. Together they enable adaptive persuasion through prompt composition alone, with no parameter updates. To support this setting, we introduce PERSIST (PERSona-driven InSurance Interactions over Time), a dataset of 60 curated personas spanning 10+ years of motor insurance renewal interactions, with probabilistic life events that shift negotiation behavior and receptiveness across sessions, verified through strict human-in-the-loop annotation. MERIT surpasses memory and experience-based baselines on every metric across two policy backbones, reaching persuasive-appeal scores of 4.10 and 4.74 (out of 5).

items.title: Grounding Collaborative Agents in Group Cognition
items.abstract: Collaborative agents joining an ongoing team rely on shared context to connect multi-party interaction histories with downstream coordination decisions. Existing work typically focuses either on retrieving historical facts from conversation logs, which surfaces isolated evidence without capturing who knows or owns what, or on evaluating end-to-end interactions, which conflates preparation with execution and lacks direct supervision because a team's history has no single ground-truth summary. To bridge this gap, we formulate group briefing, the task of reconstructing task-relevant group cognition across participants' expressed beliefs, group dynamics, and grounding gaps, and introduce a four-domain benchmark of 1,351 requests and 9,975 verified reference points paired with a two-stage evaluation pipeline combining reference-point coverage and downstream collaboration simulation. Using this pipeline, we show that GroupBrief, a simple task-guided approach that iteratively probes the message history and synthesizes a structured brief without offline memory indexing or graph construction, outperforms ten retrieval and agent-memory baselines in overall coverage with gpt-5.4-mini, while benchmarking nine language models reveals that prospective friction remains harder to recover than past state across model scales. We further use reference-point coverage as a feedback signal for harness optimization, refining GroupBrief's retrieval and synthesis instructions while keeping model weights frozen. On held-out Test projects, GroupBrief (optimized) improves coverage by 2.54 percentage points for gpt-5.4-mini and 12.88 for gpt-5.6-luna, achieving 64.46% and 68.42% preference over no brief in downstream simulations. These results establish our benchmark and evaluation pipeline as a foundation for measuring and optimizing how collaborative agents ground in group cognition.

items.title: RUIBench: What Makes a Good Robot-Use Interface?
items.abstract: Foundation models can reason about complex physical tasks, yet translating this intelligence into reliable robot execution remains challenging. We argue that a critical, often overlooked factor is the robot-use interface (RUI), which determines how agents express and execute physical actions. To systematically study its impact, we introduce RUIBench, comprising 30 manipulation tasks across five suites spanning world knowledge, in-context learning, discovery, dynamic interaction, and contact-rich manipulation. We further develop RUIKit, a unified framework that crosses six action abstractions with two interaction forms, yielding 13 interfaces under shared perception and control. In simulation, changing only the RUI shifts a frontier agent's success rate from 45% to 81%, and that of a fine-tuned 4B model from 13% to 47%. Our analysis reveals that effective interfaces reduce unnecessary decisions while preserving essential feedback, with their benefits shaped by agent behavior and physical uncertainty. We further uncover a verification gap, where agents frequently declare success despite observable failures, revealing the need for task-level verification beyond individual actions. Together, these findings establish RUI design as a critical factor in embodied agent reliability.

items.title: Exploring Multi-Player Social Games as Verifiable Training Grounds for Large Language Models
items.abstract: The training of socially intelligent language models often relies on large language model (LLM) judges, which are expensive, noisy, and vulnerable to reward hacking. Multi-player social games offer a natural alternative: they require open-ended communication to coordinate with teammates and infer hidden roles, while their rules provide an objective outcome which can serve as a verifiable reward for training. Using three social games, we explore how much social intelligence Qwen3 models can acquire through supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). Results show that against a much stronger Gemma-3-27B model, SFT and RLVR raise the win rate of Qwen3-4B from 33% to 81% on the three trained games, and from 39% to 54% on three additional held-out games. In contrast, in-context strategies such as prompting improve the win rate of Qwen3-4B by only about 6 pp across the same games we train and evaluate on. Furthermore, we show that the gains from SFT and RLVR hold across the model sizes 1.7B, 4B, and 32B. Qualitative analyses of agent behavior show signs of stronger social intelligence; for example, trained agents tend to share information more openly, check each other's claims against public evidence, and coordinate their votes. More broadly, our results demonstrate that training LLMs on verifiable outcomes in social games can cultivate generalizable social behaviors, which offers a scalable path for building socially intelligent agents.

items.title: Reproducible Social Structure Emerges From Free-Form Interaction Among LLM Agents
items.abstract: Multi-agent LLM simulations are increasingly used as models of social systems, but most published findings are anecdotal, i.e., drawn from a single run. It is therefore unclear which observed phenomena are robust findings of the simulated system itself, and which were random events in one particular run. Here, we introduce a repeatable, goal-free, proactive multi-agent framework in which fifty persona-conditioned agents with persistent memory choose whether, with whom, and how to communicate across three social platforms. The framework supports non-perturbative measurements across temporal snapshots and repetitions. Running the same world ten times from identical initial conditions for a total of 700 hours, we find that most measured network- and agent-level parameters are stable across repetitions. Throughout a run, initially broad communication contracts into sparse sustained dyads in all ten worlds. Importantly, we find that many identical dyads re-form across worlds significantly more often than expected by chance or from agent-specific sociability alone. Static personality similarity largely fails to predict these dyads. Instead, alignment and extremity in the emotions and traits expressed during first contact predict whether a pair later forms a sustained dyad. Additionally, individual agents' emotion and trait expression in their chain-of-thought predicts their future behavior. Finally, swapping either persona prompts or accumulated memories between agents causes recipients to exhibit behavior more similar to donors. Both kinds of transplant move the recipients about 60% of the way toward its donor personality, and state-transplanted agents start behaving similar to their donor agent from their next turn on. Overall, we show that repeated worlds enable robust, statistically-grounded conclusions about emergent within-configuration behavior in agent societies.

items.title: TeamFlowRL: Online Policy Optimization of Decentralized Flow Policies for Multi-Agent Coordination
items.abstract: Complex cooperative tasks require coordinated multi-agent behavior. Offline generative policies learn expressive cooperative behaviors from trajectories but remain limited by fixed datasets. Online reinforcement learning can improve them through environment interaction. However, fine-tuning flow policies is difficult because action likelihoods are hard to compute. We propose TeamFlowRL, a two-stage framework that pretrains multi-agent flow policies offline and fine-tunes them online. We formulate team policy optimization over the complete denoising trajectories of decentralized flow policies, avoiding intractable action likelihoods. The resulting objective weights each agent's trajectory ratio with a shared team advantage and clips each ratio separately, aligning local policy updates with the common team return. Across 51 paired configurations in seven simulation groups, TeamFlowRL improves every offline initialization, with a 47.3% average gain in normalized score. It also achieves 33.1% higher average success under exploration noise than Gaussian-policy fine-tuning across 6 bimanual tasks.

items.title: Coupling-Aware Reinforcement Learning for Co-Evolving Graph Games
items.abstract: Building hydrogen station networks, electric vehicle charging grids, or vaccine distribution systems requires coordinating two separately operated graphs, demand-side facilities and the supply-side networks they depend on, where each operator's payoff depends on the other's choices. We formalize this as the Co-Evolving Graph Game (CEGG), a setting that sits between facility location, interdependent-network analysis, and graph-based multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) but is not jointly addressed by any of them. We propose Cross-Graph Attention with Policy Mirror Descent (CGA-PMD), pairing cross-graph attention, which lets each agent read only the partner-graph nodes structurally coupled to its own, with a policy mirror descent update for stable training. Across three reward domains and a range of practical network scales, we find that the structure of the coupling selects which method wins: at small scale most methods are competitive, but as scale grows or coupling becomes irregular, CGA-PMD is the one method that stays reliable: it attains the highest success count on each of five real city networks, while own-only, unmasked-attention, and Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO)-based variants degrade in distinct ways. Our theoretical analysis addresses the optimizer side: the Kullback-Leibler (KL)-regularized update admits an iteration-uniform cumulative drift bound, whereas the clip update admits no such bound on the iterations where the clip does not bind. The implementation is available at https://github.com/Mina-Kim-Github/cegg-cga-pmd.

items.title: Tacinf: A Unified Tactile Infrastructure for Robot Manipulation
items.abstract: Force-aware manipulation requires robots to infer appropriate interaction forces from task context and tactile feedback. We present Tacinf, a low-cost, modular infrastructure that enables policies to predict robot actions and fingertip forces from task language, vision, and touch. Task instructions can optionally specify the desired force level. Tacinf integrates simulation data synthesis and tactile benchmarking (Tabero), vision-tactile-language-action (VTLA) policy learning, handheld data collection using the same gripper as robot deployment (Tacumi), and task-aligned sim-to-real evaluation (Taco). Together, these components form an integrated workflow connecting data collection from multiple sources, foundation-model training, and hardware deployment. We validate each component, including the simulation data, benchmark, controller, and Tacumi, and are releasing the full stack as open source. A foundation model fine-tuned solely on tactile simulation data transfers zero-shot to different real-robot tasks. Across eight policy variants, mean task success rates are strongly correlated between simulation and the real robot (Pearson r=0.998, mean maximum rank violation MMRV=0.010). For the four policies with reported force measurements, mean grip force is higher under firm instructions than under gentle instructions on all three tasks in both domains. When both object positions and instances are randomized, a mixture of teleoperation, simulation, and Tacumi data raises mean real-robot task success from 20% with teleoperation alone to 60%.

items.title: Tether: Verified Stateful Policy Engine for System-Level Monitoring of Agents
items.abstract: Autonomous AI agents are increasingly deployed for long-running tasks that execute arbitrary shell commands or programs. However, these actions can result in unauthorized network requests or persistent, malicious changes to the user's file system, processes, or privileges. Existing defense mechanisms rely on either LLM-based monitors, which lack provable safety guarantees, or stateless policy enforcement layers, which miss multi-step data flows and execution side-effects unmodeled by the policy language (e.g., network calls initiated inside a Python script). We introduce Tether, a framework for runtime enforcement of stateful security policies over the observed side-effects of an agent's actions. Tether executes each proposed action in an ephemeral, isolated sandbox, inferring abstract action semantics from observed system calls. Tether then enforces stateful policies over these inferred semantics, permitting actions to proceed only if they comply with the policy. Policies and action semantics are defined in an embedded DSL in Lean 4 capable of expressing diverse constraints, including information flow control (IFC), access control, and network security policies. Because actions can propagate labels from sources to destinations, a single rule can enforce fine-grained IFC policies across multi-step execution flows of arbitrary length. Expressing policies in Lean enables formal verification that they satisfy global security invariants (e.g., preventing network access after reading a sensitive file). We evaluate Tether on realistic coding-agent benchmarks across both benign and adversarial trajectories. With a single policy shared across all tasks, Tether blocks 100% of in-scope attacks while maintaining a benign false-positive rate under 5%.

items.title: MERIT: Experience-Guided Memory for Long-Horizon Persona-Specific Persuasive Dialogue
items.abstract: Effective long-horizon persuasion in recurring goal-oriented settings requires more than factual memory: it must track how a user's trust, negotiation behavior, and strategic receptiveness evolve across interactions. Existing persuasive dialogue systems are largely single-session, static, and unimodal, while cross-session memory systems, though temporally aware, retain only factual content and overlook persuasion-specific dynamics. We propose MERIT (Memory-augmented Experience-Rationale for Iterative Temporal persuasion), which pairs a graph-based memory of four persuasion-specific memory types with a per-persona experience rationale library that records which strategies succeed for each user and why. Together they enable adaptive persuasion through prompt composition alone, with no parameter updates. To support this setting, we introduce PERSIST (PERSona-driven InSurance Interactions over Time), a dataset of 60 curated personas spanning 10+ years of motor insurance renewal interactions, with probabilistic life events that shift negotiation behavior and receptiveness across sessions, verified through strict human-in-the-loop annotation. MERIT surpasses memory and experience-based baselines on every metric across two policy backbones, reaching persuasive-appeal scores of 4.10 and 4.74 (out of 5).

items.title: Explainable Emotion and Mental Health Reasoning in Large Language Models Using Theories of Emotion
items.abstract: Advancements in Large Language Models (LLMs) have enabled a wide range of applications. However, their ability to simulate human-like behavior and reasoning remains unclear. While emotion detection is a better-established Natural Language Processing (NLP) task, existing approaches primarily focus on directly classifying text into predefined emotion classes, often overlooking the appraisal process that explains why an individual experiences a particular emotion in a given situation. In this work, we propose Psychology-based Chain-of-Thought (PsyCoT) reasoning, a theory-driven prompting strategy grounded in the Schachter-Singer and Cognitive Appraisal theories of emotion. We propose and evaluate PsyCoT for subjective NLP tasks, including emotion analysis, emotion intensity prediction, stress analysis, and depression severity identification. Our evaluation covers four levels of classification complexity: binary, multiclass, multi-label, and ordinal scaling, spanning 11 languages. We assess the performance of five state-of-the-art LLMs across these selected subjective NLP tasks. Experimental results demonstrate that PsyCoT prompt variants improve the standard chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting across the evaluated tasks. Across all evaluated tasks, PsyCoT yields F1 score gains ranging from 0.5% to 28.1%, depending on the model, task, and language configuration.

items.title: Exploring Multi-Player Social Games as Verifiable Training Grounds for Large Language Models
items.abstract: The training of socially intelligent language models often relies on large language model (LLM) judges, which are expensive, noisy, and vulnerable to reward hacking. Multi-player social games offer a natural alternative: they require open-ended communication to coordinate with teammates and infer hidden roles, while their rules provide an objective outcome which can serve as a verifiable reward for training. Using three social games, we explore how much social intelligence Qwen3 models can acquire through supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). Results show that against a much stronger Gemma-3-27B model, SFT and RLVR raise the win rate of Qwen3-4B from 33% to 81% on the three trained games, and from 39% to 54% on three additional held-out games. In contrast, in-context strategies such as prompting improve the win rate of Qwen3-4B by only about 6 pp across the same games we train and evaluate on. Furthermore, we show that the gains from SFT and RLVR hold across the model sizes 1.7B, 4B, and 32B. Qualitative analyses of agent behavior show signs of stronger social intelligence; for example, trained agents tend to share information more openly, check each other's claims against public evidence, and coordinate their votes. More broadly, our results demonstrate that training LLMs on verifiable outcomes in social games can cultivate generalizable social behaviors, which offers a scalable path for building socially intelligent agents.

items.title: TeamFlowRL: Online Policy Optimization of Decentralized Flow Policies for Multi-Agent Coordination
items.abstract: Complex cooperative tasks require coordinated multi-agent behavior. Offline generative policies learn expressive cooperative behaviors from trajectories but remain limited by fixed datasets. Online reinforcement learning can improve them through environment interaction. However, fine-tuning flow policies is difficult because action likelihoods are hard to compute. We propose TeamFlowRL, a two-stage framework that pretrains multi-agent flow policies offline and fine-tunes them online. We formulate team policy optimization over the complete denoising trajectories of decentralized flow policies, avoiding intractable action likelihoods. The resulting objective weights each agent's trajectory ratio with a shared team advantage and clips each ratio separately, aligning local policy updates with the common team return. Across 51 paired configurations in seven simulation groups, TeamFlowRL improves every offline initialization, with a 47.3% average gain in normalized score. It also achieves 33.1% higher average success under exploration noise than Gaussian-policy fine-tuning across 6 bimanual tasks.

items.title: Joint Detection of Constructive Speech, Hate Speech and Agreement in Online Conversations
items.abstract: Online hate speech is an ever-growing issue with negative impacts on both groups and individuals, potentially causing users to withdraw from online conversations and debate. With some prominent social media platforms reducing their moderation efforts, constructive speech has emerged as an alternative strategy for countering hate. Automated detection of constructive and hateful speech can aid monitoring and improve understanding of their prevalence and online dynamics. In this work, we collect and annotate a large dataset of English and Danish social media comments for hateful tone, constructive tone, and agreement with parent comments. We fine-tune several multilingual LLMs to classify along these three dimensions and compare context-enriched and non-context-enriched model architectures. The E5-large LLM performs best on both the context-enriched (82% average F1) and non-context-enriched (81.6% average F1) classification tasks, demonstrating the potential of multilingual LLMs for scalable detection of hateful and constructive speech across languages.

items.title: Demo2Tutorial: From Human Experience to Multimodal Software Tutorials
items.abstract: Human experience in digital environments offers a vast, underexplored resource of authentic, untrimmed interactions that contain rich procedural knowledge. We introduce Demo2Tutorial, a framework that transforms this experience captured via screen recordings and interaction logs into structured, multimodal software tutorials for teaching both humans and agents. Demo2Tutorial first collects human experience via a dedicated recorder, then parses raw experience using a multimodal Action Parser to reconstruct perception, action, and intent. A Step Planner then abstracts these steps into hierarchical task graphs representing goals and steps. Finally, a Tutorial Composer transforms the parsed experience into structured, reusable image-text instructions. We evaluate the tutorial generation quality on a new benchmark derived from official software documentation. We further demonstrate that this distilled representation benefits (i) human learning, by automatically generating multimodal tutorials, and (ii) agent learning, by improving downstream GUI-agent planning and generalization. Experiments show Demo2Tutorial produces high-quality tutorials that surpass human-authored ones and significantly outperform baseline methods, while enabling both faster human task completion and improved GUI agent planning, demonstrating that structured tutorials distilled from human experience can serve as effective knowledge representations for advancing both human learning and agent capabilities. Code and data will be available at https://github.com/showlab/Demo2Tutorial.

items.title: CapSenseBand: Sustaining Cross-Disciplinary Creativity When Stitches Must Meet Signals
items.abstract: Wearable sensing systems increasingly depend on textiles that are both materially wearable and electronically functional. Their design requires collaboration between textile designers, who reason through stitches, yarn behavior, and machine constraints, and interaction designers, who reason through electrodes, signal paths, and insulation. However, these forms of expertise do not easily translate across disciplinary boundaries. This poster presents CapSenseBand, a knitted capacitive-sensing wristband developed through a research-through-design process organized around Analysis, Synthesis, and Detailing. We document an artifact chain spanning material swatches, a rapid wearable prototype, Paper Models as shared negotiation surfaces, a double-layer knitted structure, and an insulated Swept Frequency Capacitive Sensing breakout board. We show how Paper Models functioned as boundary objects, helping collaborators externalize intent, negotiate spatial and technical constraints, and preserve disciplinary expertise while converging on a shared design. We contribute a reusable swatch-to-sleeve pattern for material-centered HCI: keep discipline-specific probes open early, then converge through artifacts that make material, spatial, and electronic decisions legible before fabrication locks them in.

items.title: CRAB-Bench: Evaluating LLM Agents under Complex Task Dependencies and Human-aligned User Simulation
items.abstract: Evaluating LLM agents in realistic service scenarios requires complex task dependencies, imperfect user behavior, and an evaluation that accommodates multiple valid solutions. We introduce CRAB-Bench (Constraint-based Realistic Agent Benchmark) and RUSE (Realistic User Simulation Engine) to address this gap. CRAB-Bench generates tasks via a constraint graph over multiple interdependent entities with structured distractors, requiring agents to reason carefully over thousands of misleading candidates where only a tiny fraction of solutions are valid. RUSE replaces cooperative, template-like simulators with realistic users grounded in human behavioral studies, instantiated across diverse personas and four behavioral dimensions. Experiments on four frontier LLM agents show that the best model achieves only 61% pass@1 on CRAB-Bench, and switching to RUSE causes further drops of up to 57%, concentrated in task-solving ability rather than conversational quality. Information Disclosure is the most damaging behavioral dimension, and agents interacting with RUSE are less likely to admit mistakes, instead masking errors through implicit corrections.

items.title: MedCUA-Bench: A Screenshot-Only Benchmark for Clinical Computer-Use Agents
items.abstract: Computer-use agents could automate repetitive screen-based clinical work, but their reliability in medical graphical user interfaces remains largely unvalidated. Existing benchmarks focus on general web or desktop tasks and underrepresent medical software, which requires domain knowledge, exhibits markedly different UI design from mainstream applications, lacks public testing environments, and demands safety validation beyond task completion. We introduce MedCUA-Bench, an interactive benchmark for clinical computer-use agents. It covers 18 clinical scenarios across 10 medical domains, reconstructed from real product manuals and open-source medical systems to capture authentic clinical interfaces while avoiding licensing and privacy constraints. Each task ships with paired intent- and step-level goals to disentangle clinical reasoning from UI execution, and is evaluated by a deterministic checker over task completion and five clinical safety dimensions. Across 23 agents, the best closed-source model reaches 54.2% strict success, while all models remain below 9% on the real OpenEMR. Open-source agents average only 2.5%, with the best reaching 16.2%. MedCUA-Bench exposes the gap between current agents and reliable clinical software use, providing a reproducible testbed for future research.

items.title: Tacinf: A Unified Tactile Infrastructure for Robot Manipulation
items.abstract: Force-aware manipulation requires robots to infer appropriate interaction forces from task context and tactile feedback. We present Tacinf, a low-cost, modular infrastructure that enables policies to predict robot actions and fingertip forces from task language, vision, and touch. Task instructions can optionally specify the desired force level. Tacinf integrates simulation data synthesis and tactile benchmarking (Tabero), vision-tactile-language-action (VTLA) policy learning, handheld data collection using the same gripper as robot deployment (Tacumi), and task-aligned sim-to-real evaluation (Taco). Together, these components form an integrated workflow connecting data collection from multiple sources, foundation-model training, and hardware deployment. We validate each component, including the simulation data, benchmark, controller, and Tacumi, and are releasing the full stack as open source. A foundation model fine-tuned solely on tactile simulation data transfers zero-shot to different real-robot tasks. Across eight policy variants, mean task success rates are strongly correlated between simulation and the real robot (Pearson r=0.998, mean maximum rank violation MMRV=0.010). For the four policies with reported force measurements, mean grip force is higher under firm instructions than under gentle instructions on all three tasks in both domains. When both object positions and instances are randomized, a mixture of teleoperation, simulation, and Tacumi data raises mean real-robot task success from 20% with teleoperation alone to 60%.

items.title: Tether: Verified Stateful Policy Engine for System-Level Monitoring of Agents
items.abstract: Autonomous AI agents are increasingly deployed for long-running tasks that execute arbitrary shell commands or programs. However, these actions can result in unauthorized network requests or persistent, malicious changes to the user's file system, processes, or privileges. Existing defense mechanisms rely on either LLM-based monitors, which lack provable safety guarantees, or stateless policy enforcement layers, which miss multi-step data flows and execution side-effects unmodeled by the policy language (e.g., network calls initiated inside a Python script). We introduce Tether, a framework for runtime enforcement of stateful security policies over the observed side-effects of an agent's actions. Tether executes each proposed action in an ephemeral, isolated sandbox, inferring abstract action semantics from observed system calls. Tether then enforces stateful policies over these inferred semantics, permitting actions to proceed only if they comply with the policy. Policies and action semantics are defined in an embedded DSL in Lean 4 capable of expressing diverse constraints, including information flow control (IFC), access control, and network security policies. Because actions can propagate labels from sources to destinations, a single rule can enforce fine-grained IFC policies across multi-step execution flows of arbitrary length. Expressing policies in Lean enables formal verification that they satisfy global security invariants (e.g., preventing network access after reading a sensitive file). We evaluate Tether on realistic coding-agent benchmarks across both benign and adversarial trajectories. With a single policy shared across all tasks, Tether blocks 100% of in-scope attacks while maintaining a benign false-positive rate under 5%.

items.title: An Experimental Apparatus for Embodied Conversational AI: A Simple Implementation Coupling a Commercial Voice AI with an Avatar
items.abstract: As generative AI becomes integrated into everyday life, understanding how avatars shape human-AI interaction and the perception of AI as a social partner is becoming increasingly important. This paper builds a research instrument on audio-output coupling, which connects the audio output of a generative AI to an external avatar. There are two implementations: the browser implementation captures the audio of a tab selected through screen sharing without installing additional software, and the desktop implementation captures the audio of the service embedded in the application. Both work with the voice AI as people ordinarily use it, and as a method neither depends on a particular service. The implementation reported here, Deskmate, generates speech state, mouth shape, and expression from low-level features such as voice-band mean amplitude, RMS, peak, and transients. Because it uses no microphone, speech recognition, or transcription, Deskmate acquires neither the user's voice nor the content of the conversation. Records of the conversation remain with the voice AI provider, but none are kept automatically on the side of Deskmate. Three interchangeable backends are provided for rendering the avatar: 3D (VRM), 2D (Live2D), and CSS. Deskmate allows researchers to manipulate avatar presentation as an experimental condition, without changing the commercial service's interface, voice, or response generation. Because conversation content is not held fixed, the estimand is the total effect, including the changes in the participant's speech and the AI's responses that the presentation brings about. A server edition, served from the researcher's server for online experiments, is also provided. The effectiveness of avatar presentation has not yet been evaluated; this paper reports the design and implementation.

items.title: MERIT: Experience-Guided Memory for Long-Horizon Persona-Specific Persuasive Dialogue
items.abstract: Effective long-horizon persuasion in recurring goal-oriented settings requires more than factual memory: it must track how a user's trust, negotiation behavior, and strategic receptiveness evolve across interactions. Existing persuasive dialogue systems are largely single-session, static, and unimodal, while cross-session memory systems, though temporally aware, retain only factual content and overlook persuasion-specific dynamics. We propose MERIT (Memory-augmented Experience-Rationale for Iterative Temporal persuasion), which pairs a graph-based memory of four persuasion-specific memory types with a per-persona experience rationale library that records which strategies succeed for each user and why. Together they enable adaptive persuasion through prompt composition alone, with no parameter updates. To support this setting, we introduce PERSIST (PERSona-driven InSurance Interactions over Time), a dataset of 60 curated personas spanning 10+ years of motor insurance renewal interactions, with probabilistic life events that shift negotiation behavior and receptiveness across sessions, verified through strict human-in-the-loop annotation. MERIT surpasses memory and experience-based baselines on every metric across two policy backbones, reaching persuasive-appeal scores of 4.10 and 4.74 (out of 5).

items.title: WASP: Continual Weight Adaptation for Streaming LLM Personalization
items.abstract: Personalized large language models (LLMs) should continually adapt to users' evolving preferences. Yet extracting preference changes from noisy interaction histories while supporting inexpensive updates remains challenging. We introduce WASP (Weight Adaptation for Streaming Personalization), a recurrent framework that captures fine-grained preferences directly from raw user interactions and generates personalized LoRA adapters without expensive per-user optimization. Specifically, WASP achieves this by training a shared hypernetwork that maintains a compact user representation and outputs adapter weights in a single forward pass. As new interactions arrive, WASP updates this representation without reprocessing full interaction history, enabling continual adaptation with per-update costs independent of history length. Experiments on personalization benchmarks and chronological interaction streams show that WASP sustains high-quality personalization over long horizons under fixed compute and storage budgets. Together, these results support efficient streaming personalization and facilitate privacy-preserving on-device deployment.

items.title: EA-Bench: Measuring information and action efficiency under imperfect instructions
items.abstract: Personal agents help users complete everyday work across digital applications. Many standard benchmarks assume that users provide sufficient information to solve a task. However, agents often encounter incomplete, distracting, or inconsistent information in practice. To systematically study agent inefficiency under such imperfect information, we introduce Efficient Action (EA)-Bench, which evaluates both tool calls and user interactions in work-related tasks. To our knowledge, it is the first benchmark to jointly evaluate tool-call efficiency and user-interaction efficiency under controlled missing, redundant, and conflicting information. We construct 63 base-task instances adapted from existing work-related benchmarks. To guide perturbation design and quantify task requirements, we represent workflows as directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) and examine node-level dependencies to identify where information can be withheld, contradicted, or supplemented with distractors. We use a two-stage validation process combining AI-assisted checks with expert screening to select 232 conditions from 792 initial candidates. We organize these tasks into Easy and Hard tracks by task complexity. Experiments show that imperfect information can reduce accuracy and increase tool-use and user-interaction costs. More concerning, several models obtain apparently correct outcomes by guessing user-specific values without confirmation, revealing potential execution unreliability in current models under imperfect user information.

items.title: RUIBench: What Makes a Good Robot-Use Interface?
items.abstract: Foundation models can reason about complex physical tasks, yet translating this intelligence into reliable robot execution remains challenging. We argue that a critical, often overlooked factor is the robot-use interface (RUI), which determines how agents express and execute physical actions. To systematically study its impact, we introduce RUIBench, comprising 30 manipulation tasks across five suites spanning world knowledge, in-context learning, discovery, dynamic interaction, and contact-rich manipulation. We further develop RUIKit, a unified framework that crosses six action abstractions with two interaction forms, yielding 13 interfaces under shared perception and control. In simulation, changing only the RUI shifts a frontier agent's success rate from 45% to 81%, and that of a fine-tuned 4B model from 13% to 47%. Our analysis reveals that effective interfaces reduce unnecessary decisions while preserving essential feedback, with their benefits shaped by agent behavior and physical uncertainty. We further uncover a verification gap, where agents frequently declare success despite observable failures, revealing the need for task-level verification beyond individual actions. Together, these findings establish RUI design as a critical factor in embodied agent reliability.

items.title: Pose-based Co-speech Gesture Detection
items.abstract: Co-speech gesture detection identifies the spans in which a speaker gestures (e.g., beat or semantic gestures) in video. As a first step in gesture annotation, it is crucial for studying human communicative behaviour. Despite the availability of automatic tools and models, co-speech gesture detection remains underexplored, and its current state of the art is unclear: existing methods have been evaluated using different datasets, experimental setups, and metrics, making their performance difficult to compare. To address this gap, we benchmark existing detectors using the same cross-validation folds across three datasets (MULTISIMO, GESRes, and CABBS), with evaluation at the frame, gesture-span, and window levels. Our results show that previously reported performance does not consistently transfer to this common evaluation setting. Performance varies substantially across datasets, particularly with gesture frequency, indicating that the task remains far from solved. We further propose a CTR-GCN + BiLSTM model that outperforms the previous best method, MPSL, on CABBS. Our results provide a more consistent basis for comparing existing approaches and highlight key challenges for future research on co-speech gesture detection.
items.llm_evidence_en: Benchmarks automated co-speech gesture recognition across datasets and evaluation levels.

items.title: Evaluating Persona Consistency in LLM User Simulators Without External Reference Annotations
items.abstract: Standard evaluations assess LLM-simulated personas against an external ground truth, such as community trait annotations, but that reference is unavailable when the persona is inferred only from a short, task-oriented chat. We ask how persona consistency can be evaluated without such a reference, and propose a self-anchored internal-consistency diagnostic: the persona describes itself once and acts twice. A Likert self-report supplies a soft internal anchor; two behavioral profiles come from constrained scenario choices scored without a judge and from open-ended responses judged by an LLM. Consistency is the correlation between the self-report and each behavioral profile, in a shared six-facet BFI-2 space. The framework compares persona-construction strategies by assessing how consistently their elicited responses reflect their self-reported traits. Across ordinary-user chats (WildChat and LMSYS) and well-documented personas with community annotations (the Personality Database, PDB), profile-enriched representations agree with the anchor more closely than a raw-dialogue baseline. On PDB, this self-anchored ordering reproduces the community-annotation ordering. The pattern is stable across answering and judge models.

items.title: Don't Sleep, Keep Watch: Proactive Perception for Computer-Use Agents
items.abstract: Computer-use agents (CUAs) built on vision-language models are increasingly entrusted with long-horizon tasks in live desktop, web, and mobile environments, where the screen keeps changing on its own. However, current CUAs lack real-time situational awareness: they perceive the environment through discrete snapshots, and the substantial inference latency of VLMs, compounded by highly dynamic interfaces, opens a perception-action gap in which the observed state frequently becomes stale before the corresponding action is executed. To bridge this gap, we present NightWatch, a plug-and-play framework that endows any CUA with continuous, temporally grounded perception without changing the agent's model, prompt, or action space. NightWatch couples the VLM agent with NightWatch-0.8B, a lightweight System-1 model that performs streaming monitoring of the interface state and keeps the agent synchronized with the evolving environment at low computational cost and latency, thereby grounding each decision in the current state rather than an outdated snapshot and reducing both stale actions and idle waiting while preserving task success. Experiments on desktop and dynamic web environments (OSWorld-Verified and DynaCU-Bench) show that NightWatch, driven by a watcher of only 0.8B parameters, reduces non-reasoning wall-clock time by 33% and wasted time by 53% on OSWorld while keeping task success on par, raises success on DynaCU-Bench from 39.5% to 44.2% with the large VLM agent, and is more efficient than passive-watching baselines such as AOI and PUSV under the same screenshot-only input, as well as a System-1 decision model more than $30\times$ its size. Overall, NightWatch demonstrates that the timing of perception is as critical as its content, marking a step toward agents that maintain continuous awareness of their environment rather than perceiving it turn by turn.

items.abstract: We propose the concept of human-data interaction (HDI) as the human manipulation, analysis, and sensemaking of large, unstructured, and complex datasets. items.title: Emotion-Aware and Context-Grounded Dialogue Agents for Personalized Video Game Interactions
items.abstract: We present ChatNPC, a game companion that dynamically personalizes its responses in real time based on players' emotional shifts to enhance user immersion. The model integrates sequential data, leveraging the dynamic nature of streams to benefit from player information, spoken lines, and in-game context. We leverage recent progress in LLMs' tool-calling capabilities to extract vital information from memory and recognize potential constraints for accurate reasoning, thereby tackling the complexity of NPC conversation scenarios. The task is divided into a game sentinel-guided agent (SeGent), a memory capability, and a chat planning tool for reasoning instantiation. The approach uses a lightweight game template as an information framework, with relevant details and a thorough reasoning layout. We conduct extensive experiments on a newly developed game dataset for in-game context NPC dialogue and demonstrate that ChatNPC sequentially captures players' emotional shifts over time; responses are more naturalistic and human-like with appropriate conversational cues, pauses, and sighs; and utterances remain faithful to the dynamics of in-game context and player actions, supporting narrative continuity.

items.title: COGENT: A Modular Cognitive Architecture for Agentic User Simulation
items.abstract: LLM-based user simulation can support interface design, accessibility research, and interactive-agent evaluation, but standard computer-use agents are optimized for task completion rather than reproducing how people perceive, reason, and act. We introduce COGENT (COGnitive agENT), a modular cognitive architecture for simulating user interaction with desktop interfaces. COGENT draws on established cognitive theories, such as Norman's action cycle and ACT-R, to enable explainable, intervenable, and modular user simulation by decomposing the simulation process into cognitive modules with explicit representations of perception, memory, user state, intentions, and action selection. We begin by presenting six intervenability demonstrations, each tracing how a single edit to memory, a user attribute, or a processing module propagates through the cognitive pipeline to produce a behavioral change. We evaluate COGENT's behavioral and attributional fidelity across three benchmarks -- AgentNetBench, A11y-CUA, and SENSE-42 -- finding that it achieves statistically significant fidelity gains over computer-use baselines in reproducing recorded human behavior and recovers the relational structure among human self-reported psychological states. Together, these demos and evaluations demonstrate COGENT's utility toward more faithful, explainable, intervenable, and modular LLM-based cognitive simulations.
